venues.d: An all-suite tower set in a green garden atop the Miraflores cliff, its rooftop pool floating over the Pacific — the city's most complete grand-hotel address.
A 1927 hacienda-style landmark, declared a national monument — colonial arches, a serious Peruvian art collection and steps from the Lima Golf Club.
A restored 1914 Belle Époque mansion in bohemian Barranco, hung with contemporary Peruvian art — the city's most characterful small luxury house.
A glass tower on the Miraflores clifftop, every room facing the Pacific — polished, reliable, big-hotel service above the Costa Verde.
A sleek modern tower in the heart of Miraflores with a rooftop pool and hot tubs — well-run, contemporary comfort near the boardwalk.
A restored 1920s republican townhouse of just nine rooms, near the ocean in Barranco's arts district — boho-chic character behind heritage walls.
Marriott's design-forward European brand in central Miraflores — clean, contemporary rooms and a rooftop bar over the district.

venues.n: The Westin Lima Hotel & Convention Center
venues.d: Peru's tallest building — a glass tower in the financial district with a heated indoor pool, spa and sweeping city views.
Mitsuharu 'Micha' Tsumura's Nikkei masterwork — Japanese precision married to Peru's Amazon and Pacific, and, as of 2025, the best restaurant on earth.
Virgilio Martínez and Pía León's journey through Peru by altitude — ingredients from the ocean floor to the high Andes, plated as a map of a country.
Pía León's own restaurant beside Central — bright, colourful, ingredient-led cooking that made her one of the most celebrated chefs in Latin America.
A small Barranco room where Venezuelan and Peruvian roots meet — Juan Luis Martínez's inventive, personal cooking on an intimate scale.
Jaime Pesaque's polished flagship — Peruvian ingredients from coast, sierra and jungle through a refined, technical lens.
Rafael Osterling's long-loved room — a diverse menu drawing on Peruvian heritage and Nikkei, and the Highest Climber of 2024.
James Berckemeyer's bright, sustainability-minded kitchen — Peruvian comfort cooking, elevated and served with ease.
Gastón Acurio's landmark cevichería — the benchmark for Lima ceviche, made to fine-dining standard in a buzzing daytime room.
The restaurant that started it all — Gastón Acurio and Astrid Gutsche's flagship in a grand San Isidro hacienda, the cradle of modern Peruvian dining.
Renzo Garibaldi's butcher-restaurant — dry-aged meats and charcuterie at a level that draws serious carnivores across the city.
Generous, old-school Lima taberna cooking — hearty portions of the city's home dishes in a warm, bustling Barranco room.
Chef Héctor Solís's ode to the northern cuisine of Chiclayo — bold, regional Peruvian cooking rarely found at this level in the capital.
Gastón Acurio's warm bodega — classic criollo home cooking and grilled dishes in an easy, tavern-like setting.
Rafael Piqueras's refined hotel dining room — modern Peruvian cooking with strong technique in a polished setting.
Gastón Acurio's anticucho and grill house — Peruvian street-food classics, especially the skewers, done with real polish.

The founding square of Lima, laid out by Pizarro in 1535 and framed by the Cathedral, the ochre Government Palace and the balconied Municipal Palace. A private guide turns one walkable block into two centuries of viceregal drama; the changing of the guard at the palace at noon is the set-piece.

The city's mother church, begun in 1535 and rebuilt after earthquakes, its carved-wood choir stalls and the tomb of Pizarro himself set behind glass in a side chapel. A quiet, air-conditioned half hour on the Plaza Mayor that even restless grandchildren settle into.

venues.n: Government Palace & Changing of the Guard
venues.d: The Casa de Pizarro, official residence of Peru's president, whose ceremonial changing of the guard each day at noon draws a scarlet-and-brass parade in the forecourt. A guided visit inside — arranged ahead — reveals the gilded state rooms behind the facade.

venues.n: Monastery of San Francisco & the Catacombs
venues.d: A butter-yellow baroque church whose underground bone-lined catacombs held tens of thousands of colonial burials, the skulls and femurs still arranged in geometric wells. Upstairs, a monumental 25,000-volume antique library rewards the reader in the family; the descent is not for the very young or claustrophobic.

The 16th-century Dominican complex that cradled the Americas' oldest university (San Marcos) and holds the relics of Peru's two great saints, Rose of Lima and Martín de Porres. Tiled cloisters and a climbable bell tower make it the calmer, less-touristed twin to San Francisco.

A colonial mansion continuously inhabited by the same family since 1535 — one of the oldest lived-in houses in the Americas — its baroque Golden Room and painted ceilings shown by private appointment. A rare, discreet look behind Lima's viceregal facades, best arranged through your advisor.

The finest surviving 18th-century mansion in the city, its Andalusian-baroque doorway crowned by two intricately carved cedar-and-mahogany Moorish balconies. Now Peru's foreign ministry, so admired chiefly from the street — a two-minute stop that photographers linger over.

venues.n: Casa Museo de Barranco murals & street art walk
venues.d: Lima's bohemian quarter is an open-air gallery of murals splashed across republican mansions and cobbled alleys, best read with a local guide who knows the artists. An unhurried, camera-friendly hour that suits teenagers and design-minded travellers alike.

venues.n: Puente de los Suspiros (Bridge of Sighs)
venues.d: A little wooden footbridge over a leafy ravine, wrapped in a wish-making legend — cross without breathing and your wish comes true — with the Pacific glinting at the end of the lane. The romantic heart of Barranco, loveliest at golden hour before dinner.

The Peruvian fashion photographer's museum in a restored 19th-century townhouse, pairing his Kate Moss and Diana portraits with a room of traditional Andean dress. A tight, stylish hour that lands especially well with fashion-literate families.

A jewel-box collection of viceregal painting, silver and Cusco-school art in an Art Nouveau seaside villa with formal gardens. Small, serene and beautifully hung — the connoisseur's museum, and a cool refuge on a bright Barranco afternoon.

After dark the quarter's republican mansions turn into design bars — Ayahuasca's Andean-glam rooms among them — pouring pisco cocktails and live jazz. A grown-up evening with a driver on call, a short hop from the coastal restaurants.

A ribbon of manicured gardens running along the Miraflores clifftops high above the Pacific, threaded with sculpture, joggers and paragliders overhead. The city's favourite sunset stroll, buggy- and grandparent-friendly, with the ocean always in view.

A clifftop garden built around Víctor Delfín's giant mosaic sculpture of embracing lovers, its curving Gaudí-style benches inlaid with lines of Peruvian love poetry. One of Lima's best-placed sunset perches, and a favourite family photo stop.

An open-air mall carved into the cliff face below the Malecón, its terraces of restaurants, cinemas and shops hanging over the surf. Handy for a late lunch or a gift for the family with the Pacific as backdrop; less a sight than a comfortable pause.

A great adobe pyramid of the pre-Inca Lima culture, built of millions of hand-shaped bricks and rising unexpectedly amid the smart residential streets. The floodlit evening tour, followed by dinner at the on-site restaurant beside the ruin, is pure Lima theatre.

Tandem flights launch off the Malecón and soar along the coast on the sea breeze, the whole city and the Pacific unrolling beneath you. A ten-minute thrill for the bolder travellers, easily watched from the parks by those who would rather keep their feet down.

The buzzing central square of Miraflores, ringed by cafés and famous for the dozens of well-fed stray cats who lounge on its lawns. A gentle, easy stop for children and an antidote to museum fatigue, with churro carts nearby.

A private, appointment-based collection of pre-Columbian textiles — Paracas embroideries and Chancay lace among them — displayed with near-museum quiet in a Miraflores house. Intimate and expert, the thread-lover's Lima; guided so the delicacy of the weaving lands.

A striking clifftop museum dedicated to the victims of Peru's 1980s–90s internal conflict, its multimedia galleries sober and beautifully sited above the sea. A serious, moving hour for adults and older teens; free to enter, never crowded.

A pre-Columbian treasure house in an 18th-century mansion wrapped in bougainvillea gardens — gold and silver of the Moche kings, a walk-through storage vault, and the famously frank erotic ceramics gallery (skippable with young children). The café on the terrace makes it an easy half-day for all ages.

Peru's leading art museum in a grand 1870s exhibition palace, tracing 3,000 years from Paracas textiles to modern Peruvian masters across 18,000 works. A civilised, well-curated hour a short drive from the Plaza Mayor, easily paced for grandparents.

venues.n: Museo Nacional de Arqueología, Antropología e Historia
venues.d: Peru's oldest and largest museum, in a colonial mansion once home to the liberators San Martín and Bolívar, holding the carved Raimondi Stele and a fine scale model of Machu Picchu. The best primer before the Sacred Valley, and a five-minute walk from the Larco.

Peru's vast new national museum, a sweeping concrete landmark beside the Pachacamac ruins south of the city, guardian of half a million artefacts from 5,000 years of pre-Columbian civilisation. Pair it with the ruins for a full, uncrowded archaeology day with a private driver.

venues.n: Gold Museum of Peru (Museo Oro del Perú)
venues.d: A private collection glittering with Moche, Chimú and Lambayeque goldwork, funerary masks and ceremonial knives, alongside a large historic-arms gallery upstairs. A dazzling, slightly old-world hour in a quiet residential district — treasure that impresses every generation.

venues.n: Circuito Mágico del Agua (Magic Water Circuit)
venues.d: Thirteen illuminated fountains — some to run through, one a 120-metre tunnel of water — culminating in a nightly laser-and-music show across a colossal jet. Guinness-recognised as the world's largest fountain complex in a park, and a guaranteed hit with children after dark.

The oldest Chinatown in Latin America, entered under a red paifang gate on Calle Capón, where century-old chifas serve the Chinese-Peruvian fusion — lomo saltado, arroz chaufa — woven into the national kitchen. A lively, flavour-led walk best done with a food guide who knows the good doors.

Virgilio Martínez's altitude-themed tasting journey up the ecosystems of Peru, from ocean floor to high Andes, backed by the Mater research kitchen — crowned the World's Best Restaurant in 2023. Book months ahead; a plant-forward menu can be arranged for vegetarian guests.

Mitsuharu Tsumura's Nikkei masterwork — Japanese precision married to Amazonian and Pacific ingredients across a long tasting menu — named the World's Best Restaurant in 2025. The city's hardest table; a warm 'Maido!' greets you at the door, and dietary needs are handled with grace.

Pía León's own restaurant beside Central in the Casa Tupac compound, a colour-drenched celebration of native Peruvian ingredients from the woman named the World's Best Female Chef. A more relaxed but no less brilliant table for the design-and-food set.

A small, buzzy Barranco kitchen of Venezuelan-Peruvian cooking that has climbed the world lists on the strength of pure flavour rather than spectacle. The insider's dinner — intimate, unfussy and easier to book than the giants.

Jaime Pesaque's refined take on modern Peruvian, drawing on ingredients from coast, Andes and Amazon in a sleek Miraflores room. A polished, reliable fine-dining choice when the top two tables are full.

Lima's defining dish — raw fish 'cooked' in lime with chilli and red onion, chased with a shot of the leche de tigre marinade — eaten at a bustling lunchtime cevichería. The essential first meal in the city; ask your guide for the vegetarian causa and criollo sides alongside.

The national cocktail — pisco, lime, sugar, egg white and bitters — shaken to a foamy crown, learned hands-on in a beachfront class or savoured at a great bar. A convivial, all-ages activity (mocktail versions for younger travellers) and a fine primer on Peru's grape spirit.

A real neighbourhood market piled with Amazonian fruits, sea bass, aji chillies and unfamiliar tubers, best explored with a chef or guide who lets you taste as you go. A vivid, grounding morning — and where many of the great restaurants shop.

The pebbly beaches at the foot of Lima's cliffs, where surfers ride the swell year-round below Miraflores and Barranco. More for the seaside drive, a beachfront lunch and watching the waves than for swimming — an easy, low-key coastal hour.

A sprawling pre-Inca and Inca pilgrimage city of pyramids and temples on a bluff above the Pacific, an easy half-day south of the centre with its own excellent site museum. The most rewarding ruins near Lima; a private guide and driver make light work of the distances.

A boat from the old port of Callao out to rocky islets where a colony of thousands of sea lions lives, with a wetsuit-clad swim among the curious pups the highlight. A salt-and-adrenaline half-day for confident swimmers — a nearer stand-in for the Ballestas.

The once-rough port district's historic core, reborn as a street-art and gallery quarter, with the genteel sea-facing promenade of La Punta nearby and the star-shaped Real Felipe fortress guarding the bay. An offbeat, guided afternoon for travellers who have already ticked the classics.

venues.n: Barranco to Chorrillos coastal walk & the fisherman's pier
venues.d: South of Barranco the clifftop path drops to Chorrillos, where a small working fishing harbour, the Regatas beach club and fresh-off-the-boat ceviche shacks give a more local seaside afternoon. A relaxed, guided coastal ramble away from the tourist core.
Alonso Palomino and Gabriela León's product-driven bar — Amazonian fruits, Andean potatoes and pisco turned into some of the world's finest drinks.
Aaron Díaz's meticulously built temple to the cocktail in upscale San Isidro — a seven-drink 'Gran Carnaval' tasting of house specialities.
A rambling, beautifully restored 19th-century mansion in Barranco — countless rooms of period detail, pisco cocktails and a genuine sense of place.
A living museum to Peru's national spirit — dozens of piscos and every variation on the pisco sour, in a lively Barranco room.
A glass pavilion right on the Barranco beachfront — cocktails and Pacific sunsets at the water's edge below the cliffs.
An ingredient-obsessed cocktail bar from an alumnus of the city's best kitchens — precise, produce-led drinks in an intimate Barranco room.

venues.n: Bar Inglés — Country Club Lima Hotel
venues.d: The clubby, wood-panelled English bar of the 1927 Country Club hotel — polished pisco sours under a serious Peruvian art collection.
